--- title: "Cross-validation" description: "Cross-validation scores a model on sites it was not fitted to, from one prediction per station. When the same folds also choose the model, the winner's score is too good: a search over 100 sets of inputs keeps random columns, and nested cross-validation scores the choosing as well." order: 1 categories: [validation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## The folds that choose a model cannot also score it [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) chose a tree's node size by cross-validation by site, and noted that the winner's error was a little flattering, being the lowest of 12. With a hundred candidates, the winner can carry columns of pure noise. This page shows how to report a cross-validated score honestly when the same folds also chose the model. That matters most when a survey is too small to set test sites aside, which is common in marine work. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Out-of-fold predictions are pooled into one score In cross-validation each station is predicted once, by the model fitted without its site. That prediction is the station's **out-of-fold prediction**. Pooling the out-of-fold predictions of every station and working out one RMSE from them gives the **pooled score**. [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) averaged the folds' own RMSEs instead. With five or ten folds of sites the two barely differ, but the pooled score has one advantage: any scheme that holds out every station once scores the same stations, so pooled scores from different schemes can be compared. [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) relies on this. ## Nested cross-validation scores the search as well Choosing among candidates is part of building a model, whether the candidates are settings, sets of inputs or methods. A search scores every candidate by cross-validation and keeps the lowest. But each score is partly luck: these folds happen to suit some candidates more than others. The lowest of many scores gathers the most luck, so the more candidates there are, the more the winner's score flatters it. This is **selection optimism**. **Nested cross-validation** measures what the whole search is worth. An outer cross-validation holds out one fold of sites at a time. Inside each outer round the search runs in full on the remaining sites, with inner folds of its own, and chooses a candidate. The chosen candidate is fitted to those sites and scored on the outer fold, which played no part in the choice. The outer folds' predictions, pooled, score the search: how well a model chosen this way predicts new sites. ::: {.diagram} ![Nested cross-validation. In each outer round, one fold of sites is held out and the search runs on the rest, scoring every candidate on inner folds of its own. The candidate it chooses is fitted to those sites and predicts the outer fold once. The outer folds' predictions, pooled into one score, score the search.](img/nested-cross-validation.svg){fig-alt="In outer round 1 of 5, the first of five folds of sites is held out and the other four are handed to the search. The search cuts those four folds into inner folds; in each inner round one inner fold is held out and every candidate is scored on it. The candidate with the lowest inner error is chosen, fitted to all four folds and used once to predict the outer fold. Three steps follow: repeat for each of the five outer folds; pool the outer folds' predictions into one score; that score is the search's, choice included. A note says the outer fold plays no part in the choice, so its error is not flattered by it."} ::: A search therefore produces three things that are easy to confuse. The winner's cross-validated score tells you which candidate to keep. The nested score is the one to report. The final model, the winner refitted to all the data, has no score of its own: the nested score is the best guess at how it will do on new sites. ## Worked example The model is linear regression from [Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd), quick enough to fit thousands of times. Nested cross-validation needs no test sites, so this page uses all the survey's sites. Every fold holds whole sites, as in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). ### Preparing the data `fit_resamples()` fits a workflow in every round of the folds, and with `save_pred = TRUE` it keeps the out-of-fold predictions; `collect_predictions()` gathers them, one per station. In scikit-learn, `cross_val_predict()` does both. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude") # linear regression on any set of inputs, with gaps filled inside each round linear_on <- function(vars, data) { recipe(reformulate(vars, "abundance"), data = data) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> workflow(linear_reg()) } cross_validate <- function(vars, data, folds) { fit_resamples(linear_on(vars, data), folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse), control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) } # one RMSE from every station's out-of-fold prediction pooled_rmse <- function(rounds) { collect_predictions(rounds) |> rmse(abundance, .pred) |> pull(.estimate) } tibble(stations = nrow(survey), sites = n_distinct(survey$site_id)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| sites| |--------:|-----:| | 800| 160|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() sites = survey["site_id"] inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] # linear regression on any set of inputs, with gaps filled inside each round def linear_on(columns): numeric = [c for c in columns if c not in categorical] nominal = [c for c in columns if c in categorical] steps = [ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), nominal), ] # a candidate may have no numeric or no categorical inputs recipe = ColumnTransformer([step for step in steps if step[2]]) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", LinearRegression())]) # one RMSE from every station's out-of-fold prediction def pooled_rmse(columns, data, folds, groups): predicted = cross_val_predict(linear_on(columns), data[columns], data["abundance"], cv=folds, groups=groups) return root_mean_squared_error(data["abundance"], predicted) pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "sites": [sites.nunique()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | sites | |-----------:|--------:| | 800 | 160 | ::: ::: ::: ### A search over 100 sets of inputs picks noise Twenty columns of random numbers, `noise_1` to `noise_20`, are added to the survey. They carry no information about the catch. A search then draws 100 candidates, each linear regression on five of the 28 columns, and scores every candidate by ten-fold cross-validation by site. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(21) noise <- matrix(rnorm(nrow(survey) * 20), ncol = 20, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("noise_", 1:20))) noisy <- bind_cols(survey, as_tibble(noise)) columns <- c(inputs, colnames(noise)) candidates <- map(1:100, \(i) sample(columns, 5)) folds <- group_vfold_cv(noisy, group = site_id, v = 10) searched <- map_dbl(candidates, \(vars) pooled_rmse(cross_validate(vars, noisy, folds))) winner <- candidates[[which.min(searched)]] tibble(best = min(searched), median = median(searched), worst = max(searched)) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| best| median| worst| |----:|------:|-----:| | 4.51| 4.71| 4.82|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} winner ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "latitude" "chlorophyll_mg_m3" "longitude" #> [4] "noise_7" "noise_6" ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(21) noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.standard_normal((len(survey), 20)), columns=[f"noise_{i}" for i in range(1, 21)]) noisy = pd.concat([survey, noise], axis=1) columns = inputs + list(noise.columns) candidates = [[str(c) for c in rng.choice(columns, 5, replace=False)] for i in range(100)] folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=21) searched = np.array([pooled_rmse(c, noisy, folds, sites) for c in candidates]) winner = candidates[searched.argmin()] print(pd.DataFrame({"best": [searched.min()], "median": [np.median(searched)], "worst": [searched.max()]}).round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> best median worst #> 0 4.42 4.69 4.81 ``` ::: ```{.python .cell-code} winner ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> ['longitude', 'noise_13', 'substrate', 'noise_3', 'chlorophyll_mg_m3'] ``` ::: ::: ::: The winner scores 4.51, the lowest of the 100, and two of its five columns are noise. Its real inputs, `latitude`, `chlorophyll_mg_m3` and `longitude`, carry what skill it has; the noise columns ride along because they happened to suit these folds. How much of its lead over the median candidate, 4.71, is luck is what the next part measures. ### Linear regression on the eight inputs beats the search's choice The search is now run inside an outer five-fold cross-validation by site, with five inner folds. For comparison, linear regression on the eight measured inputs, with no search, is fitted and scored on the same outer folds. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(32) outer <- group_vfold_cv(noisy, group = site_id, v = 5) nested <- map(outer$splits, \(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) held <- assessment(s) inner <- group_vfold_cv(fitting, group = site_id, v = 5) inner_rmse <- map_dbl(candidates, \(vars) pooled_rmse(cross_validate(vars, fitting, inner))) chosen <- candidates[[which.min(inner_rmse)]] predict_held <- function(vars) { predict(fit(linear_on(vars, fitting), fitting), held)$.pred } tibble(abundance = held$abundance, claimed = min(inner_rmse), searched = predict_held(chosen), eight_inputs = predict_held(inputs), noise_chosen = sum(str_starts(chosen, "noise"))) }) |> list_rbind(names_to = "outer_fold") nested |> summarise(`search claimed` = first(claimed), `search's choice, outer fold` = rmse_vec(abundance, searched), `eight inputs, outer fold` = rmse_vec(abundance, eight_inputs), `noise columns chosen` = first(noise_chosen), .by = outer_fold) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| outer_fold| search claimed| search's choice, outer fold| eight inputs, outer fold| noise columns chosen| |----------:|--------------:|---------------------------:|------------------------:|--------------------:| | 1| 4.62| 3.56| 3.37| 2| | 2| 4.24| 4.98| 5.02| 2| | 3| 4.63| 3.98| 3.87| 2| | 4| 4.23| 5.17| 5.10| 2| | 5| 4.41| 4.50| 4.30| 2|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} outer = GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=32) rounds = [] for k, (fit_rows, held_rows) in enumerate(outer.split(noisy, groups=sites), start=1): fitting, held = noisy.iloc[fit_rows], noisy.iloc[held_rows] inner = GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=k) inner_rmse = np.array([pooled_rmse(c, fitting, inner, fitting["site_id"]) for c in candidates]) chosen = candidates[inner_rmse.argmin()] def predict_held(columns): fitted = linear_on(columns).fit(fitting[columns], fitting["abundance"]) return fitted.predict(held[columns]) rounds.append(pd.DataFrame({ "outer_fold": k, "abundance": held["abundance"].to_numpy(), "claimed": inner_rmse.min(), "searched": predict_held(chosen), "eight_inputs": predict_held(inputs), "noise_chosen": sum(c.startswith("noise") for c in chosen)})) nested = pd.concat(rounds, ignore_index=True) (nested.groupby("outer_fold") .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({ "search claimed": g["claimed"].iloc[0], "search's choice, outer fold": root_mean_squared_error(g["abundance"], g["searched"]), "eight inputs, outer fold": root_mean_squared_error(g["abundance"], g["eight_inputs"]), "noise columns chosen": g["noise_chosen"].iloc[0]}), include_groups=False) .reset_index() .round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | outer_fold | search claimed | search's choice, outer fold | eight inputs, outer fold | noise columns chosen | |-------------:|-----------------:|------------------------------:|---------------------------:|-----------------------:| | 1 | 4.48 | 4.04 | 3.87 | 2 | | 2 | 4.28 | 5.33 | 4.98 | 3 | | 3 | 4.41 | 4.35 | 4.46 | 2 | | 4 | 4.48 | 4.27 | 4.07 | 2 | | 5 | 4.64 | 4.33 | 4.11 | 2 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} per_fold |> pivot_longer(c(claimed, searched, eight), names_to = "score", values_to = "rmse") |> mutate(score = factor(score, c("claimed", "searched", "eight"), c("Search claimed", "Search's choice on the outer fold", "Eight inputs, no search, on the outer fold")), outer_fold = factor(outer_fold, 5:1)) |> ggplot(aes(rmse, outer_fold)) + geom_line(aes(group = outer_fold), colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_point(aes(colour = score, shape = score), size = 3.2) + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("grey", "vermilion", "blue")])) + scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16, 16)) + labs(x = "RMSE (individuals)", y = "Outer fold", colour = NULL, shape = NULL, title = paste("Eight inputs with no search beat the search's choice in", wins_words, "folds")) + guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Each outer fold of the nested cross-validation: the error the search claimed for its choice on the inner folds, the error of that choice on the outer fold, and the error of linear regression on the eight measured inputs, with no search, on the same outer fold.](cross-validation_files/figure-html/fig-nested-1.png){#fig-nested fig-alt='A dot plot with the five outer folds down the side and RMSE in individuals along the bottom. Each fold has three points. The search\'s claimed errors average 4.43. On the outer folds the search\'s choice lands to the right of its claim in three of the five folds, and the model on the eight inputs lands to the left of the search\'s choice in four of the five.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: The search claimed an average error of 4.43 on its inner folds. Pooled over the outer folds, the models it chose score 4.46: that is the nested score, and the honest figure for a model found by this search. On a single outer fold the choice can do better than claimed, because some folds hold sites that are easier to predict; pooled over all five, it does 0.04 worse. That is a small gap: with 800 stations and a model as simple as linear regression, luck moves the scores little. The search still did harm. In every outer round, two of the five columns it chose were noise. Linear regression on the eight measured inputs, with no search at all, scores 4.37 on the same outer folds, and beats the search's choice in four of the five. The search did not find a better model; it found the candidates that suited its folds best. Selection optimism grows with the number of candidates and with how flexible the models are, and shrinks with the number of sites. A search over many settings of a flexible model on a few dozen sites can flatter its winner badly, and only a nested score shows by how much. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Each station's **out-of-fold prediction** comes from the model fitted without its site, and the **pooled score** is one RMSE over all of them. - The winner of a search has the lowest of many scores, and part of its lead is luck: **selection optimism**. It grows with more candidates, more flexible models and fewer sites. Here a search over 100 sets of inputs kept random columns. - **Nested cross-validation** runs the whole search inside each outer round and scores its choice on the outer fold. It put the search at 4.46, a little worse than claimed and behind the eight measured inputs with no search (4.37). Report the nested score, not the winner's. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Add the eight measured inputs to the candidates as a 101st set. Does the search choose it, and how far does the nested score move? 2. Draw 1,000 candidates instead of 100. Does the winner's claimed score fall, and does the nested score follow it? 3. Run the search and the nested cross-validation on 40 sites drawn at random. Predict first: does the gap between the claimed and the nested score grow?
